prose.summary: A chef runs the kitchen's output, not just their own station: the menu, the food cost, the line, and whether ticket times hold at 8pm on a Saturday. That's the difference from a cook, who executes a station within someone else's system. The chef built the system, prices it, and answers for it when the walk-in fridge dies on a Friday.
prose.day_to_day: Most weeks split between prep and service on one side and paperwork on the other: ordering from three or four suppliers, checking invoices against what got delivered, writing next week's specials around what's cheap right now. You're on your feet for the bulk of it, expediting during the rush and tasting everything that leaves the pass. There's a stretch most days, usually mid-afternoon before service, when the kitchen is quiet and you can think about the menu instead of just running it. The part people look forward to is the first plate of a new dish coming back clean, no returns, no adjustments needed. Training runs constantly in the background: a new line cook learning to hold a sauté pan without babying it, a dishwasher moving up to prep. By Sunday night you've touched food safety logs, a budget spreadsheet, and probably a broken piece of equipment, in that order of urgency.
prose.work_environment: The kitchen is hot, loud during service, and physically demanding in a way that doesn't show up on paper: concrete floors, standing for ten hours, lifting stock pots you wouldn't want to lift twice. Hours run early to late, with weekends and holidays as the busiest shifts rather than time off. Remote work sits at 3% for a reason that needs no explanation: you can't run a line from your kitchen at home. Bad weeks are holiday season, a broken walk-in during a heat wave, or being two cooks short on a Friday with a full book.
prose.getting_in: Formal education shows up as required in only 16 of measured postings and preferred in 1, so a culinary degree helps but isn't the gate most employers care about. What they want instead is time on a line: the median experience asked for is 3 years, and that's the step that takes the longest, because you can't compress kitchen hours. The common place people stall is trying to jump straight from line cook to chef without first running a shift as sous or kitchen manager, which is where you learn ordering and costing rather than just cooking. Culinary school (roughly a year, sometimes two) can shorten the early climb by teaching knife work and technique faster than trial and error would, but it doesn't replace the years of service under your belt. Apprenticing under a working chef, in a real kitchen, on real covers, is the other accepted path, and for a lot of working chefs it's the only one they took.
prose.ladder: Early on you're responsible for your station and maybe a shift; the first real step up, usually into sous chef, means you're responsible for the whole line's output on a given night, not just your own. From there the ladder forks: one branch stays hands-on and pushes toward executive chef, owning the menu and the kitchen's identity, the other moves toward operations and multi-unit management, where you're costing and staffing across locations instead of expediting tickets. That fork tends to show up somewhere in years four to seven, once you've run a kitchen solo for a stretch. Higher up you carry less tongs-in-hand time and more responsibility for food cost percentage, supplier relationships, and whether the concept still makes sense a year from now.
prose.suits: People who come alive here are the ones who like solving a puzzle five times a night under time pressure: table six needs the risotto in four minutes, table nine just added a dairy allergy, and somehow both get handled without the pass falling apart. If you like the moment a new hire finally nails the technique you've been drilling into them for three weeks, or the specific pleasure of a supplier delivering perfect fish on a day you built a special around it, this holds your attention for years. People who leave are usually the ones who wanted regular hours or weekends with their family and didn't realize how completely a kitchen swallows both. That's not a failure of character, it's a mismatch nobody explained clearly enough before they signed on.
prose.misconceptions: Outsiders assume the job is mostly cooking; it's mostly management of people, inventory, and margin, with cooking as maybe a third of the actual hours once you're running the kitchen. Another one: that a chef's title means creative freedom over the menu. In most kitchens the menu is constrained hard by food cost targets and what your suppliers can reliably deliver, so the creativity is more like solving within a box than painting outside one.
prose.who_qualifies: Cooks are the closest match by a wide margin, sharing 65% of what the role asks for, since they already know the line, the heat, and the pace, and mainly need to add costing, ordering, and staff management. Hotel managers (19% match) bring operations and budgeting skills that transfer well but usually lack hands-on kitchen technique, which takes real time to build. Sommeliers (18%) carry food and beverage sense but come from the front of house, not the line, so the physical kitchen skills are the gap. Flight attendants (15%) are the weakest fit here, bringing service instinct but almost nothing kitchen-specific.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: The postings can't measure how a kitchen's culture holds up under a bad Saturday, and that's often what determines whether good cooks stay two years or ten. They also can't show you the burn scars, the standing pain by year five, or the specific relief of a supplier finally showing up on time after a month of scrambling.

steps.do: Get on a working line as a cook
steps.how: Take a line cook job at any real-volume kitchen, even a mid-range one, and spend 9 to 16 months learning stations under pressure. You're done with this step when you can run two stations at once during a rush without falling behind.

steps.do: Consider a culinary program, roughly a year
steps.how: A culinary certificate or associate program (commonly 12 to 18 months) compresses knife skills, technique, and food safety knowledge that would otherwise take years to pick up piecemeal. It's optional given only 16% of postings require a degree, but it shortens the early climb noticeably.

steps.do: Move into a sous chef role
steps.how: Once you're solid on the line, target a sous position where you run a full shift, not just a station. This usually takes 2 to 4 years of combined cook and line experience to land, and you know you're ready when you're already the person others ask when the head chef isn't around.

steps.do: Learn costing, ordering, and food safety compliance
steps.how: Shadow whoever handles invoices, supplier calls, and food cost percentage in your current kitchen; ask to take over one supplier relationship as practice. This is unglamorous and takes a few months to get comfortable with, but it's what separates a cook who can cook from a chef who can run a kitchen.

steps.do: Take a head chef or kitchen manager job
steps.how: Apply once you've run service solo as sous for at least a year and can speak concretely about food cost percentage and staffing in an interview. Median experience asked for across postings is 3 years, so this is realistically a 3 to 6 year journey from your first line job.

prose.tools: Food safety certification and food-service fundamentals show up in roughly half of postings and are the real gatekeepers: without them you don't get past the first screen. Kitchen management, catering, and menu development skills matter more as you move up, and procurement and budgeting show up specifically for people running the ordering and cost side. The tooling itself is still mostly physical (knives, combi ovens, inventory sheets) though POS and inventory software are creeping into more kitchen manager postings as chains standardize their back-office work.

industries.name: Independent restaurants
industries.note: Highest creative range on the menu but the tightest margins, so food cost discipline matters more here than almost anywhere else.

industries.name: Hotels and resorts
industries.note: More structure, more banquet and catering work, and often better benefits, but the menu answers to a broader guest base rather than a chef's own concept.

industries.name: Catering and events
industries.note: Volume cooking for fixed headcounts and fixed times, less improvisation during service since the whole menu is planned weeks out.

industries.name: Corporate and institutional kitchens
industries.note: More predictable hours than restaurants, often weekdays only, in exchange for less menu freedom and a more standardized food-safety process.

specializations.name: Executive chef, multi-unit
specializations.why: Chains and hotel groups are hiring for chefs who can standardize a menu across locations while holding food cost consistent, which pays more than running a single kitchen but trades away daily hands-on cooking.

specializations.name: Catering and banquet chef
specializations.why: Catering shows up in 17% of postings and is one of the more stable paths since events are booked and paid for in advance, which smooths out the feast-or-famine swings of a la carte restaurant work.

specializations.name: Kitchen manager / operations chef
specializations.why: Employers increasingly want someone who can run procurement and budgeting as well as the line; this is the fastest route to a management salary without leaving hospitality for hotel administration entirely.

pros: The moment a dish you developed goes out clean across a full service, with no sends back, is a specific kind of satisfaction that doesn't fade with repetition.
You can taste, adjust, and fix your own mistakes in real time, which is rare in work where most output takes days to see the result of.
Kitchen skill is portable across countries and concepts; a chef who can run a line in Geneva can run one in Toronto.
Training a cook who arrived barely able to hold a knife into someone who can run their own station is visible progress you get to watch happen.
cons: The physical toll (burns, standing all day, lifting heavy pots) accumulates in ways that show up as joint and back problems by your forties.
Weekends and holidays are your busiest shifts, not your time off, and that doesn't change much as you move up.
Margins in most kitchens are thin enough that a bad month of food cost can mean cutting your own staff's hours.
Pay at the median (around $62k) is modest relative to the hours and physical demand, and it takes years of line experience before it moves meaningfully higher.

faq.q: how long does it take to become a chef
faq.a: Most people need 3 to 6 years from their first line cook job to a head chef or kitchen manager title, since the median experience employers ask for is 3 years and that time can't be compressed. Culinary school can shorten the technique-learning curve by about a year, but it doesn't replace time running a line.

faq.q: do you need a culinary degree to be a chef
faq.a: No: only 16% of postings require one and just 1% even list it as preferred. What employers screen for is years on a line and food safety knowledge, so a strong apprenticeship under a working chef can substitute for a degree entirely.

faq.q: chef vs cook, what's the difference
faq.a: A cook executes a station within a system someone else designed; a chef designed the system, sets the menu, prices the food cost, and answers for the kitchen's results. The jump from one to the other is the single most common early-career move in this field, at 62% match on skills but a real drop in salary and responsibility until you build kitchen management experience.

faq.q: can a chef job be remote
faq.a: No, in practice: remote share sits at 3% because the work requires physical presence at a stove, a walk-in, and a line during service. The rare remote-adjacent roles are usually menu consulting or corporate recipe development, not kitchen chef roles.

faq.q: is being a chef a good career right now
faq.a: It depends heavily on what you want from work: the median pay ($62k) is modest for the physical demand, but the day-to-day problem-solving and visible craft keep a lot of people in it for decades. It suits people who want tangible daily results over people who want predictable hours or high pay early on.
